description: Friction - what causes it, what it depends on, and where it helps and harms.

slides.heading: What is friction?
bullets: A force that opposes motion between two surfaces in contact.
It always acts opposite to the direction of motion.
Caused by tiny bumps and irregularities on every surface.
Even smooth-looking surfaces are rough under a microscope.
slides.notes: Slide a book across the desk and let it stop. Ask what force stopped it.

slides.heading: What friction depends on
bullets: How rough or smooth the two surfaces are.
How hard the surfaces are pressed together (weight).
Rougher surfaces and heavier objects give more friction.
It does not depend on the area of contact.
slides.notes: Have students rub hands gently, then press hard and rub - they feel more friction and heat.

slides.heading: Types of friction
bullets: Static friction - acts when the object is still and about to move.
Sliding friction - acts when one surface slides over another.
Rolling friction - acts when an object rolls; it is the smallest.
That is why wheels and ball bearings are used.
slides.notes: Push a heavy box: hardest to start (static), easier to keep sliding, easiest on rollers.

slides.heading: Friction is a friend
bullets: Lets us walk without slipping.
Lets vehicles start, turn and brake.
Lets us hold a pen, strike a matchstick, tie a knot.
Lets nails hold and lets us write on paper.
slides.notes: Ask what would happen in a world with no friction - nothing could be held or stopped.

slides.heading: Friction is a foe
bullets: Wears out shoe soles, tyres and machine parts.
Produces heat and wastes energy in machines.
Slows moving objects and reduces efficiency.
Needs extra fuel to overcome it.
slides.notes: Point to a worn tyre or an old shoe sole as everyday evidence.

slides.heading: Increasing and reducing friction
bullets: Increase: treads on tyres and soles, spikes on sports shoes.
Reduce: oil, grease and lubricants between surfaces.
Reduce: ball bearings to change sliding into rolling.
Reduce: smooth, streamlined shapes for vehicles.
slides.notes: Match each method to a real object the students have seen.

slides.heading: Quick recap
bullets: Friction opposes motion between touching surfaces.
More for rough surfaces and heavier objects.
Rolling friction < sliding friction < static friction.
We increase it for grip and reduce it with lubricants.
slides.notes: Four students, one point each, to close.
